svg.title: Competing Consumers
svg.desc: Competing Consumers. Several workers pull from one queue, so work is shared and throughput scales out. Step 1, One consumer falls behind: Jobs arrive at 10/s and the only worker does 4/s, so the queue grows by 6 every second. Step 2, Add consumers, one queue: Three workers share one queue; each message goes to just one of them. 12/s, so the backlog drains. Step 3, A worker dies mid-job: Worker 2 crashes holding m-41. Its lease runs out, m-41 is visible again and worker 3 processes it. Step 4, What you give up: order: m-50 and m-51 both update order 7 and finish out of order. Where order matters, route by key.

g.text: Jobs arrive at 10/s and the only worker does 4/s, so the queue grows by 6 every second.
Three workers share one queue; each message goes to just one of them. 12/s, so the backlog drains.
Worker 2 crashes holding m-41. Its lease runs out, m-41 is visible again and worker 3 processes it.
m-50 and m-51 both update order 7 and finish out of order. Where order matters, route by key.
One worker takes the next job only when it has finished one.
Each message goes to one worker and is hidden from the
others until that worker acks it or its lease runs out.
m-41 stays hidden while its lease runs, though no one is
working on it. Then the broker makes it visible again.
m-50 and m-51 are both updates to order 7.
10 jobs arrive every second; each worker finishes 4
Every job is kept, but each one waits longer than the last.
One worker is a ceiling: 4 jobs a second, however long the
queue gets. A faster machine only raises that ceiling.
A queue: each message to one worker.
Publish-subscribe: a copy for every one.
Nothing is lost, but m-41 was delivered twice and worker 2
may have done part of it. Make processing idempotent.
A message that keeps failing is moved to a dead-letter
queue after a set number of receives, so it stops coming back.
✕ out of order: m-50 was sent first
Where it matters: one consumer per key
Parallelism ≤ number of keys or partitions.
